title: VB8-07318
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Ghana, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated November 9, 2018, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Ghana, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated November 9, 2018, rejecting his claim for refugee protection.

The Appellant seeks refugee protection in Canada because he fears persecution in Ghana because his friend is a homosexual. The RPD found that the claimant was not credible. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment. I will consider each alleged error in the analysis below.
Based on my independent review of the facts of the case, I agree with the RPD and I find that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The determinative issue in this case is whether the RPD erred in its credibility assessment.

When reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. I may defer to the RPD's credibility assessment of oral testimony, if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.2 Reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage. NEW EVIDENCE The new evidence does not meet the criteria to be admitted

In order to be considered, new evidence must meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)3 and the Singh/Raza4 factors being credibility, relevance and newness.

Subsection 110(4) states that new evidence may only be presented at the RAD if the proposed new evidence arose after the rejection of the claim or; it was not reasonably available at the time of the rejection or; that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time of the rejection. In terms of evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim, it is the content of the evidence and not the date of the document that is determinative. With respect to the admissibility of new evidence, the burden lies with the Appellant. The RAD applies a narrow interpretation of subsection 110(4). This is not an opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD.5 It is expected that full and detailed submissions on the admissibility and the relevance of the proposed new evidence will be included.6

The Appellant seeks to introduce a letter from Iman XXXX XXXX XXXX that purports to clarify dates in a letter that was previously submitted in evidence at the RPD. New evidence cannot be submitted at the RAD to repair credibility concerns with evidence that has already been submitted to the RPD. The Appellant has also not provided any explanation for why this could not have been reasonably available and submitted before the RPD decision. The new evidence is not admitted. ANALYSIS The RPD did not err in taking a negative inference from the Appellant's failure to disclose that he had lived in Brazil

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that he was not a credible witness because he failed to disclose that he had lived in Brazil prior to 2016. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by not accepting his explanation and by not considering the circumstances under which the Appellant completed his Basis of Claim (BOC)7 form. I do not agree. After the Minister intervened with evidence that the Appellant had lived in Brazil, the Appellant told the RPD that he had lived in Brazil from XXXX 2014 to XXXX XXXX, 2015. The Appellant explained that he neglected to mention the fact previously because he was focused on the countries he was in after his troubles started and he did not consider it necessary to list his time in Brazil on his BOC.

I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's explanation does not suffice to explain why he omitted a significant fact. The BOC form clearly states that claimants are to provide as much detail as possible regarding their claim and the accompanying general application form requires claimants to list all countries in which they have lived for more than six months in the five years prior to arriving in Canada. The Appellant's residence history in Brazil is particularly relevant to the Appellant's claim because it includes the period leading up to his alleged trouble with his brother and also serves to establish his presence in, or absence from, Ghana. The RPD found that the omission of his residency in Brazil was sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness. I agree and I find that the Appellant has forfeited the presumption of truthfulness.

The Appellant stated he lost his passport and he has not submitted other documentary evidence to establish his whereabouts from 2014 to 2016. The RPD concluded that there is no credible evidence to establish that the Appellant travelled back to Ghana from Brazil and that he was in Ghana in 2016 when he alleges he suffered an assault instigated by his brother. After my independent assessment of the evidence, I agree with the RPD. The RPD did not err in taking a negative inference from inconsistencies regarding when Michael's sexual orientation became known

The Appellant argues that he provided reasonable explanation for discrepancies as to the time his brother found out about that the Appellant's friend, XXXX, was homosexual. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in not accepting his explanation.

The Appellant testified that he has had problems with his family because of his association with XXXX for a long time stretching back at least to 2004 when he was in high school. The Appellant states in his BOC narrative that his brother found out that the Appellant's friend, XXXX, was gay at the end of 2015 and then his brother began harassing the Appellant at that time. The Appellant explained the discrepancy by stating that he wrote 2015 because that was when problems with his brother escalated.

The RPD fully considered the Appellant's explanation in the RPD Reasons. The RPD did not find that the explanation was adequate given the centrality of the issue to the Appellant's case. I agree with the RPD and find the Appellant does not adequately explain the discrepancy in the timing as to when his family, which included his brother, found out about XXXX sexual orientation .As mentioned earlier, the Appellant stated in his BOC that the alleged attack by his brother happened after his brother found out about XXXX sexual orientation at the end of 2015, but the Appellant then testified that problems with his family regarding XXXX sexual orientation began in 2004. Therefore, I find that the RPD did not err in taking a negative credibility inference. The RPD did not err in finding that the account of the assault upon the Appellant and his subsequent escape relied on a series of chance events

The Appellant argues that it was an error for the RPD to find that the Appellant's story regarding the attack against him and his escape is not plausible. The Appellant cites case law8 that the RPD must justify a finding of implausibility. In its decision, the RPD cites case law9 that the RPD can conclude that a narrative is not believable if it relies on a series of events of chance that are fortuitous in nature.

The RPD questioned the Appellant regarding the incident in which he was assaulted by a crowd led by his brother. The RPD found the Appellant's narrative regarding the assault was not plausible. The Appellant testified that he was attacked in his home by a very large number of individuals armed with knives and cutlass sticks with the stated intent of killing him. The Appellant maintained that he was able to push the attackers aside, escape through a bedroom window that had been removed previously, scale a wall, and readily find a cab that was willing to take him to his friend's house notwithstanding that the Appellant did not have money for payment.

When questioned by the RPD, the Appellant was not able to estimate the number of assailants or to provide further details as to how the attack unfolded. The attack in question is central to the Appellant's story as to how he came to claim refugee protection. The Appellant did not provide additional details regarding his escape over the wall and the how he subsequently found a taxi. While it is entirely understandable that this episode would be one of high emotional involvement for the Appellant, it is reasonable to expect that some, if not all, of the details would be clearly etched in his memory given that this episode is what prompted him to seek refugee protection.

The RPD noted that there was no documentary evidence to corroborate the events as described or the injuries suffered by the Appellant. Given that the usual presumption of truthfulness had already been rebutted, the RPD was correct to expect corroboration. It would be reasonable to expect that the Appellant provide medical reports, police reports, or witness affidavits to corroborate some of the key events in his narrative. I agree with the RPD's assessment. The Appellant's narrative relies on a series of chance events that are fortuitous in nature and I find that the RPD did not err by finding that the narrative is not credible. The RPD did not err in finding a general lack of credibility on the part of Appellant

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding a general lack of credibility on the part of the Appellant. The Appellant argues that he provided a reasonable explanation as to why he had not amended his BOC regarding his residence in Brazil and that the RPD erred in not accepting this explanation.

As discussed above, the RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation that he was focused on events that occurred since the problems with his brother and therefore did not include his Brazil residency. The Appellant also testified that issues with his wife contributed to his omission of his Brazil residency however he did not provide a clear explanation as to how this was so when he was questioned on the point at the RPD.

The RPD questioned the Appellant regarding the circumstances under which he lost his Ghanaian passport. The Appellant testified that he could not be sure when and where he lost his passport. He initially testified that the passport and his other documents got lost while he was on a boat in Columbia, he then testified that he really did not know where they were lost. He testified that the journey was so arduous that he was not focused at the time on his personal documents and belongings but rather on saving his life. The Appellant provided general details only when questioned at the RPD concerning the journey during which he lost his passport. I agree with the RPD. Both the passport and circumstances under which it was lost during his journey to Canada are central to his claim. The Appellant testified that his journey to Canada was arduous and harrowing yet he is unable to provide more than general details. He is also vague as to how he lost some identity documents but preserved others. The RPD did not err in its assessment of the documentary evidence.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant was not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection notwithstanding that the RPD found that the Appellant is not a credible witness. The Appellant cites case law that in some circumstances a case for refugee protection can succeed on the basis of other credible evidence even if the Appellant's testimony is found not credible

While the Appellant's argument may be true in certain situations, the onus is still always on the Appellant to adduce either his own evidence, or independent objective evidence that is sufficient and credible, to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, he meets the criteria for refugee protection in Canada. The RPD considered all the evidence before it.

The RPD fully canvassed a media article reprinted from the internet. The RPD gave the Appellant a chance to respond to the RPD's credibility concerns with respect to the article on the second day of the hearing. The RPD found that there is no reliable evidence that the article was produced by a credible news agency. The Appellant did not challenge the RPD's finding on appeal. I agree with the RPD and I accord little weight to the article.

In the present case, the Appellant relies on a letter from an Iman, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and an affidavit from his wife, XXXX XXXX. The letter from the Iman states that the Appellant is gay and counsels him to stay away from Ghana. The letter provides no detail regarding how the Iman knows the facts to which he is attesting. The RPD found that an apparent discrepancy with dates in the letter detracts from its credibility. The Appellant did not challenge the RPD's findings on appeal but rather sought to admit new evidence to clarify the dates in the Iman's affidavit. I agree with the RPD. I find that the letter is of little probative value in establishing the facts of the case.

The Appellant has submitted an unsigned affidavit from his wife, XXXX XXXX. In the affidavit his wife refers to harassment from local hooligans and her denial to local authorities that the Appellant is homosexual. She concludes the affidavit by counselling the Appellant to stay away. The RPD gave the statutory declaration low weight because it is unsigned. The Appellant did not challenge the RPD's finding on appeal. I agree with RPD and I give the affidavit low weight.

The RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant is not a credible witness. Given that the Appellant relies heavily on his own testimony to make his case, which I agree with the RPD is not credible due to inconsistencies and implausibility, I find that the Appellant has not adduced sufficient credible evidence to meet his burden of proof to establish a claim for refugee protection in Canada.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
